title: NBA Finals draws historic viewership for New York Knicks vs. San Antonio Spurs
content:
As it turns out, big markets in sports do draw big audiences. As do big stars. (Quite literally.)

So viewers have come to their television screens by the millions to watch Jalen Brunson lead the New York Knicks against transcendent San Antonio Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama in the franchise’s first NBA Finals since 1999. The Knicks are looking to break a 53-year championship drought, with the 7-foot-4 Wembanyama standing in the way in his first career playoffs.

ESPN released the viewership numbers from Wednesday’s Game 1, and its average of 16.93 million viewers on ABC made it the most-watched NBA Finals Game 1 since 2018. A peak audience of 19.63 million tuned in to watch Brunson and the Knicks claim a 105-95 victory over Wemby and the Spurs in San Antonio. It represented a 90 percent year-over-year increase from Game 1 between the Oklahoma City Thunder and Indiana Pacers last season.

The Big Apple attracts big attention — and big dollars. Ticket prices for Game 3 in New York soared past $4,500 for the cheapest nosebleed seats as of Monday before the start of the series.

Knicks fans, including celebrity supporters such as Fat Joe, Spike Lee and Ben Stiller, have invaded opposing arenas throughout the Knicks’ run to the finals, and they made their presence known during Game 1 in San Antonio. Their cheers have often been audible to those in attendance, as well as over the broadcast.

The expanded audience has been a theme throughout both the Knicks’ playoff push, a surge that stood at 12 consecutive wins heading into Friday night, and Wembanyama’s rise to postseason stardom. The NBA posted on Twitter that these playoffs have been the most watched in 28 years, averaging 5.3 million viewers per game across the broadcast and streaming services carrying the games.

The league also announced that the Western Conference Finals between the Spurs and Oklahoma City Thunder was the most-watched conference finals in 24 years. An average of 10.8 million tuned in per game on NBC/Peacock, with Game 7 amassing an average of 15.9 million and a peak of 17.7 million viewers.

With New York on the verge of history, and Wemby seemingly making history of his own every night, millions are craning their necks to watch. In the city that never sleeps and beyond, they have captured the spotlight.

In this week’s edition of The Athletic’s MoneyCall sports business newsletter, I took a look at some NBA Finals TV comps to try to get a sense of how big this number could get, given that it involved a franchise that drives tons of fan interest and a player easily tabbed as the NBA’s most intriguing.

In 1999 (call it “Knicks-Spurs I”), that series averaged 16.1 million viewers. Big, but then again, it was an entirely different media era, if not multiple media eras, ago.

The gold standard is 2016 and 2017 — peak Warriors-Cavaliers rivalry, with the two most popular NBA players of the 21st century: LeBron James and Steph Curry. That averaged 20.3 million, the highest since the end of the Jordan Era in the late 1990s.

I thought a potentially good comp was Celtics-Lakers in 2008, which featured the league’s best historic rivalry and was slightly ahead of our social media-powered, attention-atomized era. That delivered a solid average of 14.9 million viewers.

This mighty 16.9 million number for Game 1 speaks to the truly unique convening power between the can’t-miss narcissism of the New York basketball experience and fans’ first (finals) contact with Wembanyama — a combination that, if only briefly, cuts through the clutter and reminds us all of the NBA’s annual June position within a bygone monoculture.

I fully expect that Game 2 will top Game 1, and that Game 3 in New York — with all of its attendant vibes, celebrities and $8,000 “cheap seats” — will soar even higher. Whether the series runs short or all the way to Game 7, the perfect storm of sports TV will continue. — Dan Shanoff
